meta.title: Selekoa historical research sample
meta.scope: Selected historical records, 1965–2024, plus prior roles with unknown dates. Genesis source checks are dated 2026-09-17; personnel-continuity checks are dated 2026-09-18. Human source review pending. Not a current or comprehensive sector inventory. Governance version histories through July 2026, researched September 18, 2026; policy text is not evidence of implementation. Selected capital and compute records through April 2026; transaction stages do not imply current arrangements or realised spending. Targeted corrections dated 2026-09-25: one attributed claim accepted after explicit human source review; a second narrowly scoped résumé passage is human-reviewed. Other seed claims remain pending. Intellectual Lineage II adds selected oversight citations and agenda reception, checked 2026-09-25; all new records remain pending human review. Evaluation Institutions I adds bounded institutional and documentary records, checked 2026-09-27; new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted. Evaluation Ontology I adds four scoped engagement and institutional announcement seeds, checked 2026-09-28; no human acceptance or legal succession inferred. Schema 2.7 records each source's language; the frontier safety framework sources also record the nearest existing Internet Archive capture, checked 2026-10-03. A capture shows only what the archive held on its date and does not authenticate earlier bytes. Schema 2.8 adds quoted framework provisions, recorded absences, provision-level changes and the first contested assessments to the frontier safety frameworks collection, together with Meta and Microsoft framework families, checked 2026-10-03; provisions describe what editions state, not implementation. Schema 2.9 adds control-structure and external-commitment records; its first topic, California SB 53 as chaptered (enactment, 19 quoted provisions and four framework editions that link themselves to it in their own words), was checked 2026-10-04. A commitment or legal obligation is never evidence of compliance, and no record states that the statute applies to a named company. Schema 2.10 records assessments as questions posed by Selekoa rather than statements of a source, and dates an assessment by what it assesses, never by the publication window of its sources (corrected 2026-10-05). Schema 2.11 adds propositions and the first human-thought collection: located texts from 1863 to 2022 that articulate, contest or bear on propositions about machine intelligence, each with its role and register, checked 2026-10-06. "Earliest located" means the earliest text found by the recorded searches; no record claims a first use, an origin or an influence. Schema 2.12 adds a collection of Eliezer Yudkowsky’s documented arguments about common claims on advanced AI, 1996–2026: dated passages that state, contest or bear on 29 generically phrased propositions, with engagement, retrospective reports and context-only passages marked, admitted 2026-10-08 from a machine-prepared and machine-audited candidate pack. A record says what a text states, not whether it is right. The 2026-10-10 frontier-governance increment adds selected provisions of the EU AI Act as published in 2024 and of the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendments that bear on general-purpose AI model providers, and the New York RAISE Act as announced by the Governor; checked 2026-10-10, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and Regulation texts describe duties, not compliance. The 2026-10-11 frontier-governance increment adds Commission guidelines, the training-content template, further chapters of the EU Code, a draft implementing regulation on proceedings, the New York Chapter 96 text and a Chinese generative-AI measure; checked 2026-10-11, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and texts describe duties, not compliance. Schema 2.13 adds a collection on the economics of machine intelligence: dated passages from 1952 to 2024 that state, contest or bear on 19 generically phrased propositions about explosive growth and about how mainstream economics treated automation and AI, with each text’s source tier, model conditions and stated estimates, admitted 2026-10-14 from two machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate packs. A record says what a text states, not whether an argument or model is right.

claims.subject: butler-1865-lucubratio-ebria
claims.statement: The unsigned 1865 article "Lucubratio Ebria" rejects a previous correspondent’s view that machines are separate beings whose final triumph over mankind should be expected, and treats them as the means by which the human organism develops.

time.note: Issue date of The Press, vol. VIII, issue 847, p. 2, in the Papers Past record.

claims.qualification: The article frames itself as a dream after "a single glass of hot whisky and water" and closes by leaving "our dream", which bears on reading the reply as Butler’s own position. Its attribution to Butler rests on its close match with the limbs passage of Erewhon (1872); Butler’s 1901 preface mentions an untitled second Press article that appeared "shortly after the first", whereas this one appeared two years later. It attributes the growing change in people’s physical status to people with mechanical limbs, not to machines.

thought.qualifier: Disputes the premise that machines are a separate kind of being that could triumph over people.

claims.subject: erewhon-1872
claims.statement: In Erewhon, the one serious reply to the "Book of the Machines" holds that machines are part of man’s own physical nature, "nothing but extra-corporeal limbs", and so denies the rival-kingdom premise of the treatise’s argument.

time.note: Year on the title page of the inspected 1872 Trübner printing (Smithsonian Libraries copy, catalogued as the first edition). Butler’s later prefaces give March 1872.

claims.qualification: Both voices are fiction. The narrator says the treatise’s author was thought to have the best of it, and that Erewhon destroyed the inventions of the preceding 271 years.

thought.qualifier: Inside the novel: machines as extra-corporeal limbs, not rivals.

claims.subject: samuel-1960-refutation
claims.statement: The indexed abstract of Samuel’s 1960 reply to Wiener denies that the machine is a threat to humanity, says it has no will of its own, and describes its conclusions as the logical consequences of its inputs.

time.note: Issue date in the PubMed record (PMID 17797013).

claims.qualification: Bounded to the abstract: whether it reproduces Samuel’s words or an editorial summary is not established, and the article body was not read. The statement that conclusions follow from the input does not engage Wiener’s specification half and is compatible with it.

thought.qualifier: The abstract disputes the threat and will premise of the control half.

attested.note: The abstract as indexed by PubMed, retrieved 2026-10-06. The printed pages were not retrieved, and who wrote the abstract is not established.

claims.subject: michie-1968-computer-servant-or-master
claims.statement: Michie’s essay divides tasks among human value decisions, machine detail work and cooperation, and expects computers to work as assistants rather than simply as masters or servants.

time.note: Year of first publication in Theoria to Theory 2, pp. 242–249, as given in the 1986 reprint’s acknowledgements; the 1968 pages were not retrieved.

claims.qualification: A contrary forecast, not a demonstration that advanced machines stay controllable.

thought.qualifier: Disputes the servant-or-master framing.

attested.note: Wording checked in the reprint, chapter 20 of On Machine Intelligence, 2nd edition (1986). The author says little was revised; the 1968 text was not compared.

claims.subject: drexler-1986-engines-of-creation
claims.statement: Engines of Creation argues that redundancy, design diversity and mental parts that reject actions on ethical grounds can make AI systems reliable, and that safety does not require every AI system to be trustworthy if some are and help plan precautions for the rest.

time.note: Year of the book, as given by its copyright notice; an October 1986 review is recorded in Moravec’s bibliography.

claims.qualification: A proposed approach, not proof that it works; it does not deny every possibility of losing control.

thought.qualifier: Disputes that trustworthy advanced systems are infeasible.

attested.note: Wording checked in the Foresight Institute’s web edition (© 1986 K. Eric Drexler; published for the web by Russell Whitaker), whose earliest captures are of 1997-07-09; a reader’s message of October 1996 on the site shows the edition was online by then. Not compared with the 1986 printing.

claims.subject: franzen-1992-real-life-turing-test-reply
claims.statement: Franzen’s 1992 reply says people often infer understanding from sparse or vacuous responses, and that a Turing test is only a test when conducted by someone who knows what they are doing.

time.note: Date header 11 Feb 92 10:29:03 GMT; the reply cites Rosenfelder’s message of 10 February.

claims.qualification: A defence of competent testing, not a claim that these results show intelligence.

thought.qualifier: Disputes the inference from a badly run test to the insufficiency of a competent one.

claims.subject: mccullough-1992-real-life-turing-test-reply
claims.statement: McCullough’s 1992 reply denies that the Boston competition was a serious conversation test, and argues that the judges who were not fooled show that humans and computers could be distinguished by behavioural tests.

time.note: Date header Fri, 14 Feb 1992 18:57:49 GMT; the Message-ID agrees.

claims.qualification: Relies on the same reported split of judges, which is not independently verified.

thought.qualifier: The split among judges is offered as evidence that behavioural tests can still tell machines apart.

claims.qualification: It disputes the single-leader premise of Bostrom’s scenario, not concealment itself.

thought.qualifier: Disputes that any one AI would be far ahead of the rest.

claims.qualification: It contests the inference, not the possibility of faster growth.

thought.qualifier: Contests the inference from feedback to a break with history.

claims.subject: more-1998-singularity-meets-economy
claims.statement: Max More’s comment says that Vinge, like Good, expects an immediate intelligence explosion leading to a total transformation of the world, doubts both assumptions, and finds a move straight from human-level AI to drastically superintelligent thinkers doubtful.

time.note: Comments collected in 1998; a message of 1998-09-07 quotes another paragraph of More’s comment.

claims.qualification: More accepts that human-level AI will come. The wording is attested only from 2000. Yudkowsky’s message of 1998-09-07 credits a challenge by More with prompting Coding a Transhuman AI.

thought.qualifier: Doubts an immediate explosion and a total transformation.

attested.note: The quoted wording is attested by the earliest capture of the page, of 2000-08-17.

claims.subject: loosemore-2015-debunking-fallacies
claims.statement: Loosemore’s post concludes that doomsday scenarios such as "Smiley Tiling" involve AGIs so incoherent that they can be dismissed as extremely implausible.

time.note: Posting time 2015-05-05T02:46:34Z; the API returns no author account, but the post names its author.

claims.qualification: Loosemore’s target is a supposed "Doctrine of Logical Infallibility", not deceptive concealment; it is no general guarantee against deceptive alignment.

thought.qualifier: Contests scenarios in which good development behaviour turns catastrophic at higher capability.

claims.subject: christiano-2018-takeoff-speeds
claims.statement: Christiano’s post operationalises slow takeoff as a complete four-year interval in which world output doubles before the first one-year doubling, argues that it is more likely, and holds that recursive self-improvement, though it will lead to runaway growth, is not on its own an argument for a discontinuity.

time.note: The page shows "Posted on February 24, 2018" and an update of 27 February 2018; quotes also match the capture of 2018-02-25.

claims.qualification: A claim about the speed of the transition; the post says an intelligence explosion "seems very likely" and that it is not about whether one occurs.

thought.qualifier: Argues for slow takeoff and against a discontinuity.

claims.subject: christiano-2018-takeoff-speeds
claims.statement: Christiano’s post contrasts the fast-takeoff view that whoever builds AGI has a decisive strategic advantage with a slow takeoff, in which being twelve months ahead might give such an advantage but is about as hard as building aeroplanes thirty years before anyone else.

time.note: The page shows "Posted on February 24, 2018" and an update of 27 February 2018; quotes also match the capture of 2018-02-25.

claims.qualification: Conditional on Christiano’s slow-takeoff scenario.

thought.qualifier: Contests the decisive-advantage picture under a slow takeoff.

claims.subject: christiano-2022-where-i-agree-and-disagree
claims.statement: Christiano’s post disputes the picture of AI systems hiding their capabilities while lying in wait, arguing that SGD will aggressively select against systems that do not do impressive-looking things, so less impressive precursors should appear first.

time.note: Posting time 2022-06-19T19:15:55Z; the quotes also match a capture of the posting day.

claims.qualification: A conditional disagreement; it does not deny that concealment is possible or promise safety from good observed behaviour.

thought.qualifier: Disputes concealed capability combined with a sudden leap, not the possibility of concealment.
